extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of ancient history, chronologers, and historians evaluating ancient timelines
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter discussing methods for constructing and correcting chronologies of ancient kingdoms (especially Greek and Egyptian), critiquing earlier chronologers and recommending evidentiary standards for dating events. Focuses on distinguishing fabulous from historical ages and on using synchronisms and astronomical data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer reckoning by Olympiads and years
rubrics_metrics.description: Chronology should be reduced to a reckoning by Years and Olympiads rather than by fanciful generation-counts or inflated reign-lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author praises Timæus and later chronologers who used the Olympiads and compared multiple successions (ephors, kings, archons, priestesses, Olympic victors) to align dates; avoid relying solely on genealogical or generational reckonings which produce inconsistent long reigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Unknown, Fabulous, and Historical ages
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify periods as Unknown (no history), Fabulous (mixed with poetical fables), or Historical (free from fables) when assessing antiquity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat times before Ogyges as Unknown, between his flood and the first Olympiad as Fabulous, and after the first Olympiad as Historical; applied classification guides how much credence to give sources and narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about claims predating literacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Events said to occur more than one or two hundred years before the use of letters are of little credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because reliable public records begin only after writing is established, chronologers should distrust narratives claiming great antiquity that predate literate documentary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject inflated average reign-lengths; prefer empirical generation lengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept ancient chronologers' practice of attributing 33–46 years per reign on average; a medium of ~18–22 years per reign (or ~20 years per generation) is more credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text compares asserted long reign averages (35–46 years) with observed averages from known dynasties (e.g., Judah ~22 years, Israel ~17.25 years) and argues chronologies using excessive reign lengths are unreliable and should be corrected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use astronomical observations to fix dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Astronomical phenomena (heliacal risings/settings, solstices, eclipses, and fixed-star positions) provide firm anchors for chronology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Meton's solstice observations, the Thoth circle divided into 365 parts noting heliacal risings, and the Nabonassar era synchronization are cited as means to date events and to correct floating chronologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare multiple independent successions for reconciliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Align and cross-check different chronological lists (Olympiads, kings, archons, priestesses, lists of victors) to make consistent chronology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timæus's method of comparing ephors, kings of Sparta, archons of Athens, priestesses of Argos, and Olympic victors is recommended to reconcile dates and make the Olympiad-based reckoning coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid taking antiquity claims from native priests or local boastfulness at face value
rubrics_metrics.description: Be wary of priestly or local claims of extreme antiquity (e.g., Egyptians, Chaldæans) which often inflate ages and generations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cites Herodotus's report that Egyptian priests proclaimed enormously long chronologies (e.g., thousands of years) and warns chronologers not to accept such claims without corroborating evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronology requires prose/written historical records rather than verse
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetical verse-form writings (early Greek poetry) mix fable with history and do not provide reliable chronological frameworks; chronology becomes possible once history is written in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because early Greeks expressed opinions in verse (Orpheus, Hesiod, etc.), there could be no reliable chronology until prose histories (attributed to Cadmus Milesius, Pherecydes, etc.) emerged; thus prefer prose documentary sources for dating.
